tier_reason: RocksDB's own engineering blog post (May 26, 2021) compares integrated BlobDB with leveled and universal compaction without blob files, and with legacy BlobDB. It states the CPU (18-core Skylake DE @ 1.6 GHz) and RocksDB version (~6.18.1), but the benchmark is described only as 'a customized version of our standard benchmark suite', with no command lines, compiler or flags. First-party with partial methodology, so tier C.

corrections.hardware: 18-core Skylake DE CPU @ 1.6GHz (hyperthreading enabled), 64GB RAM, 512GB boot SSD, two 1.88TB M.2 SSDs in RAID0 for data
corrections.workload: Customized version of RocksDB's standard benchmark suite cycling through six phases (initial load with 1 TB of raw values, 16-thread overwrite, point-lookup/write mix, range-scan/write mix, read-only point lookups, read-only range scans) at six value sizes from 1KB to 1MB. It compares enable_blob_files=true (integrated BlobDB with leveled compaction) against leveled and universal compaction without blob files, on a RocksDB build equivalent to v6.18.1.
corrections.caveats: This is RocksDB's own engineering blog post, not an independent benchmark. It is a RocksDB feature measured against RocksDB's default (non-blob) configuration in the same repo. The CPU model and RocksDB version are stated, but exact benchmark command lines and compiler/build flags are not: the tool is described only as 'a customized version of our standard benchmark suite'. That caps it at tier C. BlobDB does not win everywhere: it falls behind leveled compaction on workloads involving range scans at the two smallest value sizes (1KB and 4KB), and at 1MB values it is not stall-free. The numbers are from 2021 (RocksDB ~6.18.1) and may not reflect current defaults.

notes: Every number in claimed_speedup appears verbatim on the blog post: 2.3x-4.7x initial load, 1.0-1.02 vs 1.6 write amp, 2.1x-3.5x overwrite throughput, 75-78%/83-88%/88-90% write-amp cuts, up to 1.4x/5.6x reads, and 4.6x/2.3x vs legacy BlobDB. The page says 'M.2 SSDs', not NVMe, so I fixed the hardware field. repo_url facebook/rocksdb is also the known-list RocksDB entry, so the orchestrator may want to dedupe it as a feature-of-RocksDB record. The license was verified from the README (dual GPLv2 / Apache 2.0), even though GitHub's spdx_id reports only GPL-2.0.

tier_reason: This is a peer-reviewed NeurIPS 2023 paper (arXiv 2306.02846) that measures construction time of fast PLBF / fast PLBF++ against PLBF on the Malicious URLs and EMBER datasets. Public Python code exists (src/PLBFs/), but no CPU or hardware is stated, so it is not tier A. The >50x gains are not implausible because they follow from the complexity reduction from O(N^3 k) to O(N^2 k) or O(Nk log N + Nk^2), so no cap to C applies.

corrections.claimed_speedup: The maximum speedups come from the k ablation at k=50. There, fast PLBF constructs the same data structure as PLBF 233x faster (URLs) and 199x faster (EMBER), and fast PLBF++ is 761x faster (URLs) and 500x faster (EMBER). At the paper's default setting (N=1000, k=5, including model training), fast PLBF is 50.8x/34.3x faster and fast PLBF++ is 63.1x/39.3x faster than PLBF (URLs/EMBER). Fast PLBF has memory efficiency identical to PLBF. Fast PLBF++ has up to 1.0019x (URLs) and 1.000083x (EMBER) higher false positive rate than PLBF.
corrections.caveats: Peer-reviewed (NeurIPS 2023), but the paper gives no CPU or hardware details for the construction-time numbers, so it falls short of tier A despite public code and real datasets. The comparison is against the authors' own PLBF implementation (src/PLBFs/PLBF.py) in a slightly modified framework: minimize FPR under a memory budget instead of PLBF's original objective. It is not an independent PLBF benchmark. The 233x/761x headline comes from the k=50 ablation. At the default N=1000, k=5, the gains are 34x-63x. The implementation is pure Python (a reference implementation, not a production library).

notes: The abstract and Section 5.3 of the arXiv paper both contain the 233x/761x figures, and Section 5.1 gives the smaller default-setting speedups, which I added for context. Metadata checks out: MIT license, 13 stars, last commit 2025-06-24 (stale), not a fork. The original PLBF repo (kapilvaidya24/plbf) is in known_list.txt.

tier_reason: This is a peer-reviewed, independent third-party evaluation. Crossref confirms it appeared at the 2025 44th IEEE SRDS (DOI 10.1109/SRDS69199.2025.00036). It compares NNG 1.9.0 against NanoMsg 1.1.5 and ZeroMQ 4.3.4 and states the CPU (Xeon w3-2435). The public suite's bml/Makefile builds the harness with gcc -O2, but the paper states no compiler or flags, and the build flags of the libraries under test are only implied (apt packages, plus NNG built via plain CMake). So it stays at B, not A.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the paper. The benchmark repo's bml/Makefile builds the harness with gcc -Wall -Wextra -O2. install_bml.sh installs ZeroMQ and NanoMsg from Ubuntu apt packages and builds NNG v1.9.0 with 'cmake -G Ninja ..' and no CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE (NNG 1.9.0 sets no default).
corrections.caveats: This is an independent third-party evaluation, published at IEEE SRDS 2025 (44th Symposium on Reliable Distributed Systems, DOI 10.1109/SRDS69199.2025.00036 per Crossref) and also available as arXiv 2508.07934. It has a public benchmark suite (github.com/hitachienergy/messaging-libraries-benchmark) and states the CPU model and library versions, but the paper gives no compiler or build flags. The suite's install script builds NNG with CMake and no build type, so NNG was likely compiled without optimization, while NanoMsg and ZeroMQ came from distro packages. Across the paper, NNG usually loses to ZeroMQ (highest throughput overall, ~2.9 GB/s peaks) and often to NanoMsg (best latency and CPU efficiency). The qualifying win over NanoMsg is limited to large payloads: the two largest sizes over IPC, and above ~128KB over TCP loopback.

notes: Observations 4 and 7 in the arXiv PDF match the claimed_speedup text exactly (NNG beats NanoMsg at the two largest IPC sizes; NanoMsg's TCP throughput peaks at ~1.5 GB/s at 128KB while NNG reaches ~2 GB/s). The lead's SRDS 2025 attribution is correct, as Crossref confirms, so I rewrote the caveat that said otherwise. Metadata: MIT license, 4,673 stars, not archived, not a fork. The last commit is 2026-09-21, not 2026-09-03.
